description: A bunch of guys interested in aerospace
summary:
Space Relics is an interactive space museum that tells the stories of the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. Visitors spin stylised globes of each world and open nine real landing sites, from silent robotic explorers to driverless rovers and a mirror that still answers Earth’s lasers. Each site starts as a mystery to solve, then unfolds through story chapters. Visitors collect passport stamps, flip “Did you know?” cards and take a Mission Control quiz to earn a rank.
It answers the challenge by telling each object’s story, not just listing facts: why it was sent, what it found, and why it was left behind. The nine objects, across two worlds and 57 years, show how exploration grew from robot scouts to footprints to machines that drive and fly on their own. Mission facts come from NASA’s NSSDCA records, every photo is a real image from the NASA Image and Video Library with its NASA ID credited, and landing sites use their real coordinates.
These machines carry the history of exploration, and few people ever hear their stories. Space Relics makes that history playful and accessible for students aged about 10 to 14 and curious explorers of any age.
details:
What it does?

Space Relics is a web-based museum of NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors choose a world, spin its globe, and click a marked landing site. Each site opens a story that begins with a question, then unfolds through chapters covering the mission, its purpose, its discoveries, why the equipment was left behind, and where it is now.

The nine objects.

On the Moon : Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle and the Apollo 14 laser retroreflector.

On Mars : Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity.

The problem.

Students usually meet space exploration as names, dates and distances, which are easy to forget. We wanted them to ask “wait, why?”, so each object starts with a mystery. For example, Spirit’s damaged wheel became part of an important discovery: as the rover dragged the wheel through Martian soil, it exposed silica-rich material linked to ancient hydrothermal activity.

Learning and play.

• Explore : Rotate the globes, switch between the Moon and Mars, and select landing sites placed at their real latitude and longitude.

• Discover : Each story includes a mystery, NASA photographs, a planned-versus-actual mission length bar, and a “Think about it” question.

• Collect : An Explorer Passport records each site visited.

• Test : Eight “Did you know?” cards and an eight-question Mission Control quiz that awards a rank.

How is it creative?

Instead of a catalogue, every object is a mystery with a real answer: a broken wheel that led to a discovery, a mirror on the Moon that still answers Earth’s lasers, and a rover named by a 12-year-old. Myth-busters correct popular stories, such as Opportunity’s supposed “last words”. Planned-versus-actual bars show how far missions outlived their design, and a passport and quiz turn exploring into a game.

Factors we considered.

We chose depth over breadth: nine objects, each with a real mystery, a NASA photo and a NASA record, rather than a long list. We designed for students aged 10 to 14, so the site works on phones with no login or install. Because the globes are computer-drawn, we label them as stylised illustrations and keep real NASA photos separate, so visitors always know what is real. Every photo is credited with its NASA ID.

NASA data.

Mission details, dates and final locations were researched in NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), using records 1969-059C, 1967-035A, 1971-063C, 1971-008C, 1975-075C, 1996-068A, 2003-027A, 2003-032A and 2020-052A. Photographs come from the NASA Image and Video Library and are credited with their NASA IDs. The site separates real NASA photographs from the computer-drawn globes, which are labelled as stylised illustrations.

How it works?

The site is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no framework or build step. The globes are drawn on an HTML canvas. It is hosted on Vercel, so it runs in any browser with no install or account, including on phones.

Who it is for and what we hope to achieve?

The main audience is school students aged about 10 to 14, plus teachers and space enthusiasts. We hope to make space history approachable, encourage curiosity about science and engineering, and show that equipment left behind still has scientific and historical meaning.

Next steps.

More objects (Apollo 16 and 17 rovers, Phoenix, InSight), worksheets for teachers, more languages, and offline access.

Some machines came to explore. Some stayed behind. Their stories are still here.
